title: Slowing Down
human_question: What actually happens in a single moment of seeing, hearing, or touching?
journey: Chathura spends time with people whose lives depend on noticing: craftspeople, fishers reading water, trackers, musicians, cooks.
surface: The pleasure of close attention: small sounds, textures, timing, the skill of seeing what others miss.
depth: The cognitive process (vīthi): 'I see' is a rapid sequence of mind-moments with no separate seer behind it. The seven universal factors present in every moment; doors, objects, bases and functions; the seventeen-moment lifespan of matter. Inside the process is a gap, impulsion (javana), where choice happens and action is made. This is the hinge of the whole series.

arc.opening: A craft or practice that demands total attention. Object 5 is acquired here.
arc.middle: Seeing, hearing, remembering and imagining, slowed down and taken apart through real work and real skill.
arc.closing: In the gap inside a moment there is a choice, and a choice can be good.

hands_off: In that gap we can choose goodness.

concepts.role: The 18 rootless minds (seeing, hearing, receiving, investigating): the machinery that runs before any choice.
The three rootless functional minds, including the arahant's smile.
The seven universal factors in every moment of mind: contact, feeling, perception, volition, one-pointedness, life-faculty, attention.
How the ethically variable factors combine: the neutral workforce under every mood.
Mental factors in the rootless minds.
The fourteen functions of mind, from rebirth-linking and life-continuum through seeing and impulsion to registration and death.
The six doors through which experience enters.
The objects each kind of mind can take.
The physical bases on which minds depend.
The cognitive process (vīthi): the sequence of mind-moments behind every act of perceiving.
The lifespan of ultimate realities: arising, presence, dissolution; matter lasts seventeen mind-moments.
Classification of objects by intensity, which shapes the process that follows.
The full eye-door process for a very great object: the classic seventeen-moment sequence.
Process charts: the diagrams that make a moment visible.
How cognitive processes arise.
The two processes for great objects.
The six processes for slight and very slight objects: things that barely register.
Mind-door processes: thinking, remembering, imagining.
The occasions on which mind-door processes arise.
The causes of mind-door processes.
